title: Collection.toArray(): Object[] vs typed toArray(T[]) vs toArray(IntFunction), ClassCastException gotcha
keyPoints: toArray() with no argument returns Object[]; casting it to String[] throws ClassCastException because the runtime array type is Object[]
toArray(new String[0]) returns a properly typed String[] because the JVM uses the argument as a type hint
Java 11 added toArray(IntFunction): toArray(String[]::new) is the cleanest syntax using a method reference
Passing new String[0] is faster than new String[list.size()] because the JVM's JIT compiler optimizes zero-length array creation
toArray() on an empty collection returns an empty array, not null
For primitive arrays, use stream().mapToInt().toArray() because collections cannot hold primitives directly

s1_definition.oneliner: toArray() returns Object[] that cannot be cast to a typed array; toArray(new String[0]) returns String[]; toArray(String[]::new) (Java 11) is the cleanest form.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **`toArray()`** (no argument) returns `Object[]`, even if every element is a String; casting `(String[]) list.toArray()` throws `ClassCastException` because the runtime type is `Object[]`
- **`toArray(T[] a)`** accepts a typed array as a hint; `toArray(new String[0])` returns `String[]` of the correct size
- **`toArray(IntFunction<T[]>)`** (Java 11) accepts a generator function: `toArray(String[]::new)` is equivalent to `size -> new String[size]`
- If the provided array is large enough, elements are placed into it and any extra slots are set to null; if too small, a new array of the correct type and size is created
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine dumping all account cards from a drawer into a box. `toArray()` gives you a generic box labeled "Objects" – even though every card inside is an account card, the box label says "Objects" and you cannot relabel it. `toArray(new String[0])` gives you a box labeled "Strings" from the start – the right label, the right size. `toArray(String[]::new)` is the same thing with cleaner handwriting on the label.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  toArray() variants

  list.toArray()             → Object[]       (cannot cast to String[]!)
  list.toArray(new String[0]) → String[]       (type hint, JVM optimized)
  list.toArray(String[]::new) → String[]       (Java 11, cleanest)

  How toArray(T[] a) decides:

  a.length >= list.size()?
  ├── YES → copy elements into a, set remaining slots to null, return a
  └── NO  → create new T[list.size()], copy elements, return new array

  Performance:
  new String[0]           new String[list.size()]
  ┌──────────┐            ┌──────────────────┐
  │ JIT sees │            │ Allocate array   │
  │ size = 0 │            │ Zero-init slots  │
  │ Creates  │            │ Copy elements    │
  │ optimal  │            │ (zero-init was   │
  │ array    │            │  wasted work)    │
  └──────────┘            └──────────────────┘
     ~10% faster              slightly slower
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Converting a collection to an array is one of those tasks that looks simple but has a subtle trap. The no-argument `toArray()` returns `Object[]`, and casting it to `String[]` throws ClassCastException because Java arrays carry their component type at runtime. The solution is the typed overload: `toArray(new String[0])` tells the JVM to create a `String[]`, and the JVM handles the sizing internally.

In the National Bank of India system, Rajesh uses `accounts.toArray(new String[0])` when passing a list of account numbers to a legacy JDBC API that expects a `String[]` parameter. He uses the zero-length array idiom because it is both correct and slightly faster than `new String[accounts.size()]` – the JIT compiler has a special optimization path for this pattern.

Since Java 11, the cleanest syntax is `accounts.toArray(String[]::new)`, which uses a method reference to create the array. For primitive arrays, you need streams: `list.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray()` produces an `int[]`.

Remember one sentence: never cast `toArray()` to a typed array – pass a zero-length typed array as a hint, and the JVM creates the correctly-typed result for you.
